title: Why a written code
hook: a shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old rehatnamas: earlier codes that share much and differ in detail. Your line was codes change, the guru doesn't.

A woman lands in a city she has never seen, tired, far from her family. She finds a gurdwara on a side street and doesn't know a single person inside. But at the door she already knows what to do. Shoes off. Head covered. Into the hall, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, sit with the sangat. Later, down to the langar, where she sits on the floor in a row with strangers and is fed. Nobody had to explain any of it. How does that happen, and why did Sikhs bother to write it down?
screen: `A STRANGER IN A NEW CITY.` → `SHE ALREADY KNOWS WHAT TO DO.` → `WHY WRITE IT DOWN?`

segments.voice: Four reasons. First, a written code travels. Spoken custom stays close to the village it grew in. A page can cross an ocean, be read in a new language, be taught in a basement class in a city the Gurus never saw. So Sikh families in two countries can open the same pages and find the same daily prayers, the same order for a wedding, the same form for the Ardas. One code, many homes. Second, it settles things more fairly. When two people disagree about how something should be done, they can point to a page instead of to whoever speaks loudest or has the most money. A rule on paper applies to the powerful and the poor alike. Third, it gives the newcomer a starting place. Someone learning the path, or coming back after years away, can read what is asked instead of guessing or feeling foolish. Fourth, it keeps the community in conversation. The shared code was agreed by Sikhs working together, and the Guru Panth can still discuss it. A written code doesn't replace the Guru, or love, or seva, or the remembrance of the Name. It's more like a common doorway. Families still bring their own warmth, their own food, their own way of laughing in the langar line. But the doorway is the same width wherever you find it, and anyone can walk through.
screen: `A PAGE CAN CROSS AN OCEAN.` · `POINT TO A PAGE, NOT A VOICE.` · `A STARTING PLACE FOR NEWCOMERS.` · `A COMMON DOORWAY, NOT THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE CODE, MANY HOMES.`

segments.voice: Choose one rule your household keeps that nobody ever wrote down: shoes at the door, who sits where, what gets said before a meal. Put it into one plain sentence, the way it would read for someone who just moved in, on paper or silently. Then sit with it and ask whether the sentence holds everything the habit does.
Why a written code. A shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Today's word.
Your line: one code, many homes. A page can travel where a village custom can't. Rest well.
